The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $I$ be an index
set, and let $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of classes of events
$\mathcal C_i\subseteq\mathcal F$.

The family $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when for every natural
number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and
every choice of events $A_k\in\mathcal C_{i_k}$, one has

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_k\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_k).$$

Thus independence is a finite-subfamily condition. In particular, the empty
family and every one-member family are independent.

Fix a law $P$ and an iid sample $X_1,\ldots,X_n\sim P$. For a measurable vector function $\varphi:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k$, write $P\varphi=E_P[\varphi(X)]$ and $P_n\varphi=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\varphi(X_i)$, where $P_n=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{X_i}$ is the empirical measure. For a vector remainder $R_n$, $R_n=o_P(n^{-1/2})$ means $\sqrt n R_n\to0$ in $P$-probability.

A measurable estimator sequence $\widehat\psi_n$ of $\psi(P)\in\mathbb R^k$ is **asymptotically linear at $P$** with **estimator influence function** $\varphi$ if

$$\widehat\psi_n-\psi(P)=(P_n-P)\varphi+o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

where $\varphi\in L^2_0(P)^k$: $E_P\varphi=0$ and $E_P\|\varphi\|^2<\infty$. The space $L^2_0(P)$ and its almost-sure equivalence convention are as in [[def-mean-zero-square-integrable-space]]. This definition alone does not assert regularity under local alternatives, pathwise differentiability of $\psi$, or asymptotic normality.

Let $X=(X_1,\ldots,X_p)$ be a measurable random vector in $\mathbb R^p$,
where $p\ge1$ is finite, and assume $\mathbb E\|X\|_2^2<\infty$. Define
the mean coordinatewise by $\mu_j=\mathbb E X_j$ and define the covariance
matrix by
$$\Sigma:=\mathbb E[(X-\mu)(X-\mu)^T],$$
where each entry is the expectation of the corresponding real random
variable. Write $\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\sum_{j=1}^p\Sigma_{jj}$.

The well-definedness lemma proves these expectations are finite,
$\Sigma$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, and
$\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma)=\mathbb E\|X-\mu\|_2^2$.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

derivations.claim: For each Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, $\phi^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$. The common law of the $O_i$ gives a common image law, and [F2] applied to finitely many preimage events gives independence of the images. Thus $\phi(O_1),\phi(O_2),\ldots$ are IID.
The vectors in step 1.1 have mean zero and covariance $\Sigma$ by the assumptions and [F4]. Thus [F5] gives $S_n:=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(O_i)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma)$.

The assumed expansion gives $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)=S_n+\sqrt n\,r_n$, and the asymptotically linear convention [F3] makes its scaled remainder tend to zero in probability; [F6] identifies this as $o_P(1)$. Apply [F7] with $h(x,y)=x+y$ and $c=0$ to step 2.1. This proves the asserted limit, without deriving the influence expansion.

boundaries.reason: The statement assumes d>=1 and a nonempty IID subject sequence; no empty sample sum is asserted.

reviewed.reason: The Statement fixes d>=1 and an IID subject sequence and considers normalized sample sums for positive sample sizes tending to infinity. The proof applies the IID CLT to those nonempty sums. No n=0 estimator or empty-dimensional normal law is included, so the sum detector is not a domain contradiction.

boundaries.evidence: The covariance may be zero; step 2.1 applies the singular-covariance CLT and step 3.1 does not divide by a covariance entry.
Dimension d=1 is included by the statement, and the same normalized-sum and remainder argument applies in steps 1.1–3.1.
Singular covariance, including Sigma=0, is expressly allowed by the CLT in step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: No parameter-space endpoint or ratio denominator appears in the theorem.
No local choice from a nonempty family is made; AC is inherited from the stated CLT supplier and used in step 2.1.
The theorem is a one-way implication from an assumed expansion.
No converse from asymptotic normality to an influence expansion is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Checked current steps 1.1–3.1 and all eight direct supplier carriers. Measurable preimages preserve common law and mutual independence; finite second moment identifies covariance. The IID CLT explicitly allows singular and zero covariance under AC, carried in the statement. Same-sample scaled remainder tends to zero in probability, so vector Slutsky applies to addition without independence. Fixed finite d>=1 excludes empty dimensions; sample indices tend to infinity. No converse, process limit or derivation of the expansion is claimed. Reader and refuter have no findings; no mathematical defect found.

Let S,T be metric spaces, $g:S\to T$ measurable, and $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$. If the discontinuity set $D_g$ is $\mu$-null, then $g_*\mu_n\Rightarrow g_*\mu$. Consequently $X_n\Rightarrow X$ implies $g(X_n)\Rightarrow g(X)$ whenever $P_X(D_g)=0$.

For a real random variable $X$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, its **characteristic function** is
$$\varphi_X(t)=\mathbb E[e^{itX}]=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{itx}\,\mathbb P_X(dx),\qquad t\in\mathbb R.$$
For a specified Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R$, write $\varphi_\mu(t)=\int e^{itx}\,\mu(dx)$.

The complex integral means the sum of the real integral and $i$ times the imaginary integral, as in [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]]. [[thm-change-of-variables-for-expectation]] therefore applies to this bounded Borel function and proves the displayed identity. If Borel probability laws $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ on $\mathbb R$, then $\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)$ for every real $t$.

$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi_{\mu_n}(t)\to\varphi_\mu(t)\ \text{for every }t\in\mathbb R.$$

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer and $p_\theta(x)=\theta\cdot x$ for $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R^d$ are determined by all the laws $(p_\theta)_*\mu$. $$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$

derivations.claim: For each group, measurable preimages show that $\phi_g(O_{gi})$ are IID; [F2] applied to preimages of finite event selections also shows independence across groups. Their means and covariances are $0$ and $\Sigma_g$ by assumption and [F3]. Since $\rho_g>0$ and $n\to\infty$, $n_g\to\infty$. Applying [F4] to each of the finitely many groups gives $U_{g,n}:=n_g^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(O_{gi})\Rightarrow Z_g\sim N_d(0,\Sigma_g)$.

Put $a_{g,n}=\sqrt{n/n_g}$, so $a_{g,n}\to\rho_g^{-1/2}$. Applying [F5] to the continuous map $(x,a)\mapsto ax$ gives $a_{g,n}U_{g,n}\Rightarrow\rho_g^{-1/2}Z_g$. For any fixed $u\in\mathbb R^d$, [F6] gives convergence of the projections; by [F12], $u^TZ_g$ is normal, and the affine characteristic-function identity [F9] with [F10] identifies its scaled law as $N(0,\rho_g^{-1}u^T\Sigma_gu)$, including zero projected variance.

Let $V=\sum_g\rho_g^{-1}\Sigma_g$. By [F3], $u^TVu=\sum_g\rho_g^{-1}u^T\Sigma_gu\ge0$ for every $u$, so $V$ is positive semidefinite; under [A1], [F12] supplies $Z\sim N_d(0,V)$. Set $W_n=\sum_g a_{g,n}U_{g,n}$. Fix $u\in\mathbb R^d$ and any frequency $t\in\mathbb R$. The scalar terms $u^Ta_{g,n}U_{g,n}$ are independent across $g$ by [F2]. By the characteristic-function definition [F7], weak-convergence continuity [F8], independent-sum product identity [F9], and normal formula [F10], step 2.1 gives pointwise convergence of the characteristic function of $u^TW_n$ to $\prod_{g=1}^G\exp(-t^2u^T\Sigma_gu/(2\rho_g))=\exp(-t^2u^TVu/2)$. This is the characteristic function of $u^TZ$ by [F12] and [F10]. The criterion [F11] gives $u^TW_n\Rightarrow u^TZ$.
Since step 3.1 holds for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$ and the specified target is $Z$, [F13] gives $W_n\Rightarrow Z\sim N_d(0,V)$.

The expansion in the statement is $W_n+R_n$. By [F14], $R_n=o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to the zero vector. Apply [F5] with the continuous addition map to step 4.1 to obtain the claimed estimator limit. This proof derives the group-sum limit but does not establish any consumer's expansion.

boundaries.reason: The theorem assumes fixed finite G>=2, d>=1, and positive sample sizes n_g.

reviewed.reason: The Statement requires fixed G>=2, d>=1 and positive deterministic integers n_g with positive limiting proportions. Each group sum has at least one term and n_g tends to infinity in step1.1. A quantifier over finitely many nonempty groups is not an assertion about empty groups.

boundaries.evidence: If some or all Sigma_g vanish, step 3.1 uses the zero-variance characteristic function and step 4.1 still obtains the possibly degenerate normal target.
A finite initial n_g may equal one, but step 1.1 proves n_g tends to infinity from rho_g>0; G=1 is excluded by the statement.
The covariance sum may be singular or zero; steps 3.1–4.1 do not invert it.

boundaries.reason: The allocation limits rho_g=0 or rho_g=1 are excluded by the theorem's explicit interior-proportion hypothesis.
No local selection from a nonempty family is made; AC is inherited by the normal-law, characteristic-criterion, CLT, and Cramer-Wold suppliers.
The theorem is a one-way implication from the assumed group expansion.
No converse from the Gaussian limit to the group expansion is asserted.

risk_review.notes: Independently checked steps 1.1–5.1 and all fifteen current direct suppliers. Fixed finite G and positive deterministic limiting proportions imply n_g tends to infinity; measurable images preserve within-group IID and independence of the subject-family sigma-algebras. Each group CLT carries AC and finite second moments. Deterministic scaling follows from vector Slutsky; projections are continuous. Independence gives the finite product of characteristic functions; its limit is exp(-t^2 u^T V u/2) with symmetric positive semidefinite V=sum rho_g^(-1) Sigma_g. Current normal definition and normal characteristic-function lemma include zero variance; characteristic criterion and Cramer–Wold apply to the specified Gaussian law under AC. Final same-sample o_P(1) remainder is handled by addition in Slutsky. No inverses of covariance, allocation endpoints, growing group count, process CLT, or derived estimator expansion are asserted. No mathematical defect found; reader/refuter findings are empty.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $(\mathcal O,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, and let $O_1,O_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be a measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued estimator based on $O_1,\ldots,O_n$ for a fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $\phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable, $E_P\phi=0$, and $E_P\|\phi\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $\Sigma=E_P[\phi\phi^T]$. Assume the separately established expansion, with remainder $r_n$ on the sample probability space,

$$\hat\theta_n-\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(O_i)+r_n,\qquad r_n=o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$

The remainder notation means $\sqrt n\,r_n\to_P0$, as in [[def-asymptotically-linear-estimator-and-influence-function]]. Thus $\phi$ is the estimator influence function in the asymptotically linear sense: the theorem assumes the expansion and does not establish it. The covariance may be singular, including zero.

derivations.claim: For every Borel set $C\subseteq\mathbb R$, $\{B_i-p\in C\}=\{B_i\in C+p\}$, where $C+p$ is Borel. The common law of the $B_i$ therefore gives a common law for $B_i-p$, and applying the finite independence identities in [F1] to these preimage events proves that the shifted observations are IID. The variable $\phi(B_i)=B_i-p$ has mean $p-p=0$ and variance $p(1-p)$ by [A1] and [F2]. The estimator identity $\bar B_n-p=n^{-1}\sum_i(B_i-p)$ gives the required expansion exactly, with zero remainder.

Apply [F3] with $d=1$ and $\Sigma=p(1-p)$ to obtain $\sqrt n(\bar B_n-p)\Rightarrow N(0,p(1-p))$. At $p=0$ or $p=1$, $\bar B_n=p$ almost surely, so the limit is the point mass $N(0,0)$ covered by the theorem.

boundaries.reason: The example uses n>=1 and a Bernoulli parameter p in the stated interval; an empty sample is excluded.

boundaries.evidence: At p=0 or p=1 the variance is zero and step 2.1 gives the point-mass limit N(0,0).
At p=1 each observation and the sample mean equal one; step 2.1 covers this deterministic endpoint.
At p in {0,1} the exact expansion in step 1.1 has a zero influence variance and step 2.1 remains valid.
Both parameter endpoints p=0 and p=1 are explicitly included and verified in step 2.1.

boundaries.reason: The example makes no selection from an arbitrary nonempty family.
The example verifies a direct implication, not an equivalence.
No converse is claimed.

risk_review.notes: Checked Example and Verification 1.1–2.1 against all four current direct suppliers. Shift by p is measurable and preserves mutual independence and common law. Direct Bernoulli expectation gives E(B-p)=0 and E(B-p)^2=p(1-p), finite for every p in [0,1]. Sample mean identity supplies exactly zero remainder; current IID terminal theorem applies in d=1 under explicitly inherited AC. At p=0 and p=1 all errors vanish almost surely and the limiting point mass N(0,0) is explicitly included. No empty sample or converse is asserted. Reader/refuter have no findings; no defect or repair.

The family $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when for every natural
number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and
every choice of events $A_k\in\mathcal C_{i_k}$, one has

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_k\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_k).$$

Thus independence is a finite-subfamily condition. In particular, the empty
family and every one-member family are independent.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Fix a finite $G\ge2$ and $d\ge1$. For each total sample size $n$, let $n_1,\ldots,n_G$ be positive deterministic integers with $\sum_{g=1}^G n_g=n$, and suppose $n_g/n\to\rho_g\in(0,1)$ with $\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g=1$. For group $g$, let $O_{g1},O_{g2},\ldots$ be IID with law $P_g$ on a measurable space; assume the subject families in distinct groups are independent. Let $\phi_g$ be measurable with $E_{P_g}\phi_g=0$, $E_{P_g}\|\phi_g\|_2^2<\infty$, and $\Sigma_g=E_{P_g}[\phi_g\phi_g^T]$. If a measurable estimator of fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$ has the separately established expansion, with remainder on the same sample probability space as its group sums,

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)=\sum_{g=1}^G\sqrt{\frac n{n_g}}\frac1{\sqrt{n_g}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_g}\phi_g(O_{gi})+R_n,\qquad R_n=o_P(1),$$

then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d\!\left(0,\sum_{g=1}^G\rho_g^{-1}\Sigma_g\right).$$

The group count $G$ is fixed; the laws $P_g$ may differ. The covariance may be singular. This is a terminal finite-dimensional result: it neither proves the estimator expansion nor supplies a continuous-time or functional martingale CLT.

derivations.claim: Put $\phi_1(x)=\rho(x-p_1)$ and $\phi_2(x)=(1-\rho)(x-p_2)$. The measurable maps preserve within-group identical laws and the finite event-product identities for independence across groups, so their sampled values meet [F1] and [F2], as required by [F4]. By [A1] and [F3], they are centered, square-integrable group contributions with variances $\Sigma_1=\rho^2p_1(1-p_1)$ and $\Sigma_2=(1-\rho)^2p_2(1-p_2)$. The identity $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)=\sqrt{n/n_1}\,n_1^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\phi_1(X_{1i})+\sqrt{n/n_2}\,n_2^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^{n_2}\phi_2(X_{2i})$ is exact, so its remainder is zero.

The covariance in [F4] is $\rho^{-1}\Sigma_1+(1-\rho)^{-1}\Sigma_2=\rho p_1(1-p_1)+(1-\rho)p_2(1-p_2)$. Thus $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)$ converges to the centered normal with this variance. The formula includes $p_g\in\{0,1\}$, where the corresponding group variance is zero.

boundaries.reason: The example assumes two groups, positive sample sizes, and an interior allocation fraction.

boundaries.evidence: If either Bernoulli parameter is zero or one, that group's variance term is zero in step 2.1.
The Bernoulli endpoint p_g=1 is deterministic and is included by the variance calculation in step 1.1.
If both group variances vanish, the limit covariance is zero; step 2.1 retains this case.

boundaries.reason: The allocation endpoints rho=0 and rho=1 are excluded; the theorem requires rho in (0,1).
No selection from an arbitrary nonempty family is made.
The example verifies a direct terminal-limit implication.
No converse is claimed.

risk_review.notes: Checked Example and Verification 1.1–2.1 against all five direct suppliers. The target and estimator use the same fixed rho weights, so no unassumed sqrt(n) allocation-rate remainder occurs. Contributions rho(X-p_1) and (1-rho)(X-p_2) are measurable, centered, square integrable and mutually independent across groups. The displayed expansion is exact because sqrt(n/n_g)/sqrt(n_g)=sqrt(n)/n_g. With positive limiting proportions the group theorem applies (sample means require positive sample sizes, which in any case hold eventually). Covariance simplifies to rho p_1(1-p_1)+(1-rho)p_2(1-p_2). Each p_g endpoint, one or both zero variances, is included; rho endpoints are excluded. AC is explicitly carried; no converse is claimed. Reader/refuter report no findings; no defect or repair.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space, let $I$ be an index
set, and let $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of classes of events
$\mathcal C_i\subseteq\mathcal F$.

The family $(\mathcal C_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when for every natural
number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and
every choice of events $A_k\in\mathcal C_{i_k}$, one has

$$\mathbb P\left(\bigcap_{k<n}A_k\right)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(A_k).$$

Thus independence is a finite-subfamily condition. In particular, the empty
family and every one-member family are independent.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $d\ge1$, let $(\mathcal O,\mathcal A,P)$ be a probability space, and let $O_1,O_2,\ldots$ be IID with law $P$. Let $\hat\theta_n$ be a measurable $\mathbb R^d$-valued estimator based on $O_1,\ldots,O_n$ for a fixed $\theta\in\mathbb R^d$. Suppose $\phi:\mathcal O\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable, $E_P\phi=0$, and $E_P\|\phi\|_2^2<\infty$, and set $\Sigma=E_P[\phi\phi^T]$. Assume the separately established expansion, with remainder $r_n$ on the sample probability space,

$$\hat\theta_n-\theta=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(O_i)+r_n,\qquad r_n=o_P(n^{-1/2}),$$

Then

$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$

The remainder notation means $\sqrt n\,r_n\to_P0$, as in [[def-asymptotically-linear-estimator-and-influence-function]]. Thus $\phi$ is the estimator influence function in the asymptotically linear sense: the theorem assumes the expansion and does not establish it. The covariance may be singular, including zero.

derivations.claim: For each $n\ge2$, [A1] gives $P(Y_{ni}=0)=t_n=2^{-1/n}$. The events $\{Y_{ni}=0\}$ are independent by the finite event-product identity in [F2], hence $P(K_n=0)=(2^{-1/n})^n=1/2$. Since $X_i=1$, the ratio is $1$ when $K_n>0$ and is $0$ otherwise; therefore $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-1)$ is $0$ when $K_n>0$ and $-\sqrt n$ when $K_n=0$.

For every fixed $M>0$ and every integer $n>M^2$, $P(|\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-1)|>M)=P(K_n=0)=1/2$. Taking $\eta=1/4$ in [F3] shows that the root-$n$ errors are not $O_P(1)$. If they converged in distribution, [F4] would make them $O_P(1)$, a contradiction. Under [A2], the expansion required by [F5] would imply a weak limit, so it cannot hold for this estimator. The example shows why a consumer must control its own random denominator before claiming a terminal influence limit.

boundaries.evidence: The empty risk set K_n=0 is explicitly included in the estimator definition and handled in step 1.1.
On K_n=0 the denominator is zero and the stated extension defines the estimator; step 1.1 computes this event's probability exactly.
When K_n=1 the numerator and denominator are both one, so the ratio equals one as in step 1.1.
The root-n error has a two-point law with a mass one half escaping to -infinity; step 2.1 proves it is not tight.

boundaries.reason: For n>=2 the threshold t_n=2^{-1/n} lies strictly between zero and one; endpoint thresholds are not part of this example.
The example uses no selection from a nonempty family.
The example is a one-way refutation of an unsupported root-n conclusion.

The Example fixes uniform times, threshold2^-1/n and the empty-risk ratio value0. Verification step1.1 gives empty-risk probability1/2 and step2.1 proves failure of root-n tightness. This one failure witness does not assert a converse characterization of all estimators admitting an influence expansion. The reverse boundary would require inferring the model premises from that conclusion, which this item does not claim.

risk_review.notes: Checked Example and Verification 1.1–2.1 against all six current direct suppliers. For every n>=2 the deterministic threshold t_n=2^(-1/n) is interior; uniform continuity of the event-time law makes P(T_i<t_n)=t_n. Finite independence gives P(K_n=0)=t_n^n=1/2 exactly. The explicit empty-set convention defines the ratio at denominator zero; since X_i=1 it equals one off that event and zero on it. Thus root-n error has masses 1/2 at 0 and -sqrt(n); for each fixed M>0 its eventual tail is 1/2. Taking eta=1/4 violates the stated O_P(1) definition. Current stochastic-order theorem part 3 (proof 1.1) makes any finite-dimensional weakly convergent sequence O_P(1); contradiction excludes a weak limit and hence any centered finite-variance fixed-IID influence expansion under the terminal theorem with AC. No independence across rows or process-level CLT is needed, no converse is asserted, and K_n=1 is harmless. Reader/refuter have no findings; no defect or repair.
